faq.a: The right hemidiaphragm is thinner and more prone to microscopic defects, allowing ascitic fluid to pass more easily.
faq.q: Why is hepatic hydrothorax usually right‑sided?

faq.a: They may reduce ascites but often fail to stop pleural fluid leak; procedural intervention is needed for large symptomatic effusions.
faq.q: Can diuretics alone cure hepatic hydrothorax?

faq.a: No, because continuous drainage can cause protein loss, infection, and re‑expansion pulmonary oedema; thoracentesis is preferred.

exam: A cirrhotic patient presents with sudden right‑sided dyspnoea and a large pleural effusion – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform bedside thoracentesis; fluid analysis will confirm a transudate and exclude infection.
How does hepatic hydrothorax differ from congestive heart failure effusion on examination? — Hydrothorax is usually unilateral, right‑sided, with absent peripheral oedema and normal JVP.

A patient with known hepatic hydrothorax has recurrent effusions despite optimal diuretics – what definitive treatment is indicated in low‑resource settings? — Consider TIPS if interventional radiology is available; otherwise evaluate for liver transplantation.
What feature on pleural fluid analysis most strongly supports a hepatic origin? — SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicating portal hypertension‑related transudate.
Why is a chest tube contraindicated in hepatic hydrothorax? — It leads to massive protein loss, risk of infection, and re‑expansion pulmonary oedema without addressing the underlying leak.

In a resource‑limited hospital without ultrasound, how can you confirm a hepatic hydrothorax bedside? — Use percussion and auscultation to detect shifting dullness, and perform diagnostic thoracentesis to analyse fluid.
What are red‑flag signs that a hepatic hydrothorax has become infected? — Fever, pleuritic chest pain, leukocytosis, and pleural fluid neutrophil count >250 cells/µL.
Explain why sodium restriction is essential in managing hepatic hydrothorax. — Reducing sodium limits ascitic fluid formation, decreasing the pressure driving fluid across the diaphragm.
ai.title: Hepatic Hydrothorax
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hepatic hydrothorax is a transudative pleural effusion that occurs in patients with advanced cirrhosis, usually right‑sided, due to diaphragmatic defects. It worsens breathlessness and signals decompensated portal hypertension.

b: Occurs in ~5‑10% of cirrhotics with ascites
Right‑sided in >85% of cases
Absence of primary lung disease
sections.p: In cirrhosis, high portal pressure forces ascitic fluid through microscopic diaphragmatic pores into the pleural space, most often the right hemithorax. The fluid is a transudate with low protein and lactate dehydrogenase.

b: Diagnostic criteria: cirrhosis + pleural effusion + transudate + no other cause
Stage I: small, asymptomatic; Stage II: moderate, dyspnoea on exertion; Stage III: large, refractory dyspnoea
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion, pleural fluid analysis, and exclusion of cardiac or pulmonary causes. Severity is staged by volume of effusion and impact on respiration.

t.b: Confirms effusion side and size; if unavailable, bedside percussion and auscultation can estimate fluid
Distinguishes transudate (protein <3 g/dL, LDH <0.6 × serum) from exudate; rules out infection or malignancy
Detects ascites and diaphragmatic defects; if ultrasound not available, clinical exam for shifting dullness and fluid wave
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension as the driver

b: Dyspnoea out of proportion to ascites volume
Pleural fluid that re‑accumulates rapidly after drainage
Risk of empyema when pleural fluid protein >1 g/dL
sections.p: Large hydrothorax can precipitate hypoxia, respiratory failure, and infection (spontaneous bacterial empyema). It also reflects severe portal hypertension, prompting evaluation for liver transplantation.

b: Percussion: dullness over lower lung fields, resonant above – suggests fluid
Auscultation: decreased breath sounds, egophony above fluid level
Shift of dullness with patient position confirms free fluid
sections.p: Focus on bedside assessment and rapid decision‑making when resources are limited.

b: Salt restriction <2 g/day and diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide) to reduce ascites
Therapeutic thoracentesis for symptomatic relief; limit to 1‑1.5 L at a time to avoid re‑expansion pulmonary oedema
TIPS (transjugular intra‑hepatic portosystemic shunt) if refractory and facilities exist
Consider liver transplantation for definitive cure
sections.p: Treat the underlying portal hypertension, control fluid accumulation, and consider procedural options when medical therapy fails.

t.b: Monitors re‑accumulation; if effusion recurs within 24‑48 h, consider TIPS or pleurodesis
Prevents circulatory dysfunction when >1 L removed; if albumin unavailable, monitor vitals closely

b: Congestive heart failure – exudative or transudative but bilateral and associated with elevated JVP
Tuberculous pleuritis – lymphocytic exudate, high protein, common in East Africa
Spontaneous bacterial empyema – infected hydrothorax; requires antibiotics

b: Rely on SAAG and clinical context rather than protein alone
Chest X‑ray may miss small right‑sided effusions; use bedside percussion

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in dyspnoea with fever – possible empyema
Rapid re‑accumulation after thoracentesis causing respiratory compromise
Hypotension or altered mental status after large fluid removal
